narrative:
The model predicted a 69% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. While students who are accepted typically rank around the middle of their class, you placed in the bottom decile, which the model sees as a clear warning sign for bar exam performance.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA also mattered, but they worked in the opposite direction. Both scores were somewhat below the average of accepted students (35 versus 37.2 on the LSAT, and 2.7 versus 3.23 GPA), yet they still provided a modest pull toward passing. Unfortunately, these positive signals were not strong enough to overcome the impact of your third-year ranking.

Your family income, full-time status, gender, and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the remaining part of law school. A significantly better class rank in later years, combined with strong bar-prep work, would likely change the model’s outlook and open doors to admission or reconsideration.
